analysis.one_liner: Requires background checks through licensed dealers for nearly all private firearm sales.
analysis.headline: The House passed it 227-203 on March 11, 2021, but the Senate never brought it to a vote before that Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would make it illegal for a private seller to hand a gun to another private person unless a licensed gun dealer first takes possession and runs a background check — the same check already required at gun stores. Family gifts, loans at a shooting range, hunting loans, and transfers to prevent imminent harm are exempt. It passed the House in March 2021 but never received a vote in the Senate, where it sat on a calendar until that Congress expired.
analysis.who_benefits: People at risk of gun violence — in homes, at schools, and in neighborhoods — because guns sold privately today can change hands with no check at all, including to people legally barred from owning firearms. Licensed gun dealers also gain a new stream of fee-paying business, since every private sale would have to route through one.
analysis.who_benefits_short: People at risk of gun violence; gun dealers

how_it_helps.text: Closes the 'private sale loophole': under current federal law, an unlicensed seller can transfer a firearm with no background check, so a buyer barred from gun ownership because of a felony, domestic violence record, or other disqualification can simply buy from a private seller instead of a dealer.

Uses the existing dealer-based background check system rather than building anything new: a licensed dealer, manufacturer, or importer takes possession of the firearm and processes the transfer exactly as it would a store sale.

Carves out everyday transfers that pose little risk — bona fide gifts between spouses, partners, parents, children, siblings, and grandparents; loans while target shooting, hunting, or pest control; transfers to estate executors; and temporary transfers to prevent imminent death or harm.
States explicitly that the bill cannot be construed to create a national firearms registry, and leaves state laws stricter than it intact.

analysis.who_pays: Private gun sellers and buyers, who would pay a dealer's transfer fee and take the time to complete the check for every private sale, including buyers in rural areas far from a licensed dealer. The gun lobby and many gun owners opposed the requirement as a burden on lawful transactions.

drawbacks.text: Every private sale would carry a dealer's transfer fee and paperwork, and in rural areas the nearest licensed dealer can be a long drive away — a real cost for law-abiding sellers and buyers, which critics said falls hardest on lower-income gun owners.

Opponents argued the bill addresses only one channel: people determined to obtain a gun illegally can still use stolen guns, straw purchases, or the existing secondary market, so the check adds friction for lawful owners while not stopping determined criminals.

Records of private-sale transfers would be held by dealers rather than the government, but the bill does leave the buyer subject to a dealer-mediated transaction, which some gun owners viewed as a step toward registration despite the bill's anti-registry language.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core trade-off is real: a modest fee and errand for lawful private sellers and buyers, in exchange for a check on every transfer that today can happen with no questions asked. The family, hunting, and emergency exemptions address most of the feared burdens on ordinary gun ownership, but the bill would not stop every illegal acquisition route, and its Senate defeat left the private-sale loophole fully open.

outcome.mechanism: The House passed it in March 2021, but the Senate never voted on it — it sat on the Senate calendar until that Congress expired in January 2023, and all work on the bill died with it.

narrative.text: Introduced March 1, 2021, and referred to the House Judiciary Committee; no markup was held there, but the House brought it straight to the floor under a rule in March.

The House passed it on March 11, 2021, 227-203: 219 of 220 Democrats voted yes, and only 8 of 211 Republicans did. A Republican motion to send it back to committee failed 207-217, with all 207 yes votes coming from Republicans.

The bill was received in the Senate the same day but did not even get a first reading until May 2022, when it was placed on the Senate calendar. No Senate committee took it up and no vote was ever scheduled before the Congress ended January 3, 2023.

Under Senate rules, most bills need 60 votes to reach a final vote; with Democrats holding 50 seats and Republicans 50, the bill could not have cleared that bar without significant Republican support, and none of the floor action needed to test it ever happened.
The bill's text that survives in the record is the House-passed version, placed on the Senate calendar May 25, 2022 as Calendar No. 390 — where it remained.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Private-sale sellers and the gun lobby come out ahead: the private-sale exemption from background checks remains the law today, unchanged since the bill died. Advocates for gun-violence prevention, who had waited for this measure since a similar bill passed the House in 2019, came out with nothing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Private-sale sellers and the gun lobby

for.name: Rep. Mike Thompson
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on March 1, 2021 and led it through House consideration.

for.name: 219 of 220 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Voted yes on passage, supplying 219 of the 227 votes it needed to pass the House.

for.name: 8 of 211 House Republicans
for.what_they_did: Voted yes on passage, giving the bill its bipartisan 227-vote majority.

against.name: 50 of 50 Senate Republicans
against.what_they_did: Opposed the bill in sufficient numbers that it could not reach the 60 votes needed to overcome a filibuster; no Senate vote was ever scheduled in two years.

against.name: Rep. Jim Jordan
against.what_they_did: Moved to recommit the bill to committee — a last-chance motion to kill it — which failed 207-217 before final passage.

against.name: 207 of 211 House Republicans
against.what_they_did: Voted no on passage and unanimously backed the motion to recommit that would have returned the bill to committee.

against.name: Gun rights advocacy organizations
against.what_they_did: Ran public campaigns against the bill and pressed members to oppose it, framing it as a burden on lawful gun owners.

sides.party_line_note: In the House, 219 of 220 Democrats voted yes while only 8 of 211 Republicans did — 227-203 overall — and in the Senate the bill never came close to the 60 votes it needed in a chamber split 50-50 between the parties.

industries.note: The bill would make dealers the mandatory middleman for every private transfer, locking in their gatekeeper role and adding fee revenue per sale. Their interest here runs alongside the bill's public-safety purpose.

Law-abiding private sellers and buyers would pay dealer transfer fees and take extra time for every sale — costs opponents said fall hardest on rural and lower-income gun owners — in exchange for keeping guns away from people legally barred from owning them.

industries.industry: Gun manufacturers and the gun lobby
industries.note: The bill does not restrict purchases by people who pass a check, so manufacturers' sales are largely untouched, but industry-allied advocacy groups fought the measure as a step toward restricting lawful ownership — and won, since the bill died.
